title: Hate Crimes Against Hindus in UK Rise 15%, From 182 to 210 Offences
excerpt: Home Office data for England and Wales shows 210 recorded offences targeting Hindus in the year ending March 2026, as community groups warn the count misses unreported cases.
body:
• Religiously motivated hate crimes targeting Hindus in England and Wales rose 15% in the year ending March 2026, from 182 to 210 recorded offences - an increase of 28 offences, Home Office data shows.
  • Police recorded 146,825 hate crimes overall in that year, up 7% from 137,560, while religious hate crimes rose 13% from 10,067 to 11,419 offences.
  • Hindu-targeted offences were 2% of religious hate crimes and occurred at a rate of 2 per 10,000 population, compared with 5,132 offences targeting Muslims and 3,162 targeting Jews.
  • For British Hindus: community groups say many incidents go unreported, and Hindu temples have no dedicated protection scheme and must compete for general places-of-worship funding.

Religiously motivated hate crimes targeting Hindus in Britain rose by 15% in the year ending March 2026, according to Home Office data reported by The Times of India. In absolute terms, police recorded 210 offences where the perceived targeted religion was Hindu, up from 182 the previous year - 28 more offences.

The increase came inside a broader rise. Police recorded a total of 146,825 hate crimes in England and Wales in the year ending March 2026, up 7% from 137,560 a year earlier. Religious hate crimes rose 13%, from 10,067 to 11,419 offences, and race hate crimes rose 9% to 107,926 offences.

The numbers in context

The Home Office table on perceived targeted religion puts the Hindu figure in proportion. Offences targeting Muslims rose 15% from 4,479 to 5,132, the largest absolute count at 46% of religious hate crimes. Offences targeting Jews rose 10% from 2,874 to 3,162. Offences targeting Christians rose 24% from 502 to 624, and those targeting Sikhs rose 3% from 259 to 267. Hindu-targeted offences accounted for 2% of religious hate crimes, at a rate of 2 per 10,000 population.

The absolute number for Hindus - 210 - is far smaller than the counts for Muslims and Jews. But community representatives argue it understates what Hindus experience, because non-physical incidents are less likely to be reported.

"A 15% rise should not be left as a line in a table."

- Spokesperson, INSIGHT UK

Community groups say the count misses cases

Anil Bhanot, managing director of Hindu Council UK, told The Times of India that many Hindus choose to suffer in silence when an incident is not a physical assault, and do not report it because they do not feel the authorities will act. He said Hindus were experiencing an increase in serious physical assaults, unlike the public fear, alarm or distress offences that were the most commonly recorded crimes targeting Muslims and Jews.

A spokesperson for INSIGHT UK, an advocacy group for British Hindus, made two further points in the same report. First, the Home Office written commentary accompanying the statistics discussed Jews and Muslims with no mention of Hindus, the UK's third-largest religious group. Second, on protection funding, synagogues and mosques have dedicated protection schemes while Hindu temples have none and must compete for a small share of general funding. Bhanot added that although government funding exists that Hindu temples can apply for to protect their security, historically nothing has been awarded to them.

INSIGHT UK also cited its own anti-Hindu hate survey, due to be published in November, which had 2,688 responses. According to the group, every respondent had witnessed or experienced anti-Hindu hate, ranging from physical violence and online harassment to temple vandalism and misrepresentation of Hinduism in media and education. That is a self-selecting survey, not police data, and should be read differently from the Home Office count.

What this means for British Hindus

The practical takeaway is about reporting and protection. The Home Office itself notes that police-recorded figures are a measure of demand on police, not a complete measure of prevalence, because not all hate crime is reported. For a temple committee or a family weighing whether an incident is worth reporting, the official position matters: a report is what puts an offence into the statistics that drive funding and commentary - the same statistics community groups say currently leave Hindus as a line in a table. Readers in England and Wales can read the full release and its data tables on the Home Office hate crime page.

What to watch next

Two things will test whether this release changes anything. The first is whether the Home Office commentary in future releases addresses Hindu-targeted crime directly, as INSIGHT UK is demanding. The second is protection funding: whether Hindu temples, which must currently compete for a general pot, receive awards or a dedicated route. INSIGHT UK's survey in November will add community-reported evidence alongside the police count. Until then, the verified baseline is the Home Office one: 210 recorded offences targeting Hindus in the year ending March 2026, up 28 on the year before.
